title: Battery Ecosystems: A Comparative Analysis of Lithium-Ion Tech Policy
gist: This Carnegie compendium compares lithium-ion battery industrial policy in China, South Korea, Japan, the EU, the U.S., Canada and India. China dominates: it has more than 2,000 GWh of cell capacity and roughly 90-97% of active-materials capacity, and it is now tightening export controls on advanced battery technology while pushing solid-state batteries in its 15th Five-Year Plan. Other countries' results vary widely: Korean chaebol are running at about 50% utilization, Japan is trying to recover from a collapse in market share, the EU has stalled on industrial execution after Northvolt, the U.S. has overbuilt cell capacity once EV subsidies were removed, and India has tiny output under its incentive scheme.

themes.theme: China's entrenched dominance and export-control turn

insights.claim: China's operational battery cell capacity already exceeded 2,000 GWh in 2025, more than current global demand, and as much as 5,000 GWh could be online by 2030. CATL and BYD together accounted for 65% of China's 2025 production.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: Structural global overcapacity will keep pressure on cell prices and on margins at non-Chinese producers.
insights.locator: China’s battery ecosystem is the world’s largest

insights.claim: The IEA estimated in 2024 that China held 97% of global anode active material capacity and 90% of cathode active material capacity, so its control of midstream materials exceeds even its control of cell production.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: Anyone outside China trying to build a battery supply chain faces a midstream materials bottleneck; non-Chinese CAM and AAM projects carry scarcity value.
insights.locator: China’s global role in anode active materials

insights.claim: Beijing is moving to control the outflow of battery technology. MOFCOM and MIIT finalized restrictions on LFP manufacturing technology in July 2025, MOFCOM proposed in October 2025 export controls on LFP materials and on batteries above 300 Wh/kg (later paused in U.S. trade talks), and 2026 State Council decrees tightened review of outbound investment and supply-chain security.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: OECD buyers' access to the best Chinese cells will narrow, and the overseas expansion plans of CATL and other Chinese makers become harder to execute.
insights.quote: The threshold of 300 Wh/kg for high-energy-density batteries in the proposed export controls from October 2025 is the clearest indicator so far
insights.locator: Beyond domestic market signals

insights.claim: China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) shifts political priority to solid-state batteries, while LFP enters a more market-driven phase with lower NEV purchase incentives. Anti-involution policy will trim some low-end overcapacity but will not change China's central role.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: State support in China will tilt toward solid-state projects; LFP margins will depend on market demand rather than subsidies.
insights.locator: Outlook and Signposts (China)

insights.claim: Carnegie identified 15 sodium-ion facilities in China at or near commercial scale, with nearly 100 GWh of planned capacity; BYD's Qinghai plant is the largest. Twelve lithium-metal or solid-state facilities had started pilot production by 2026, and five target energy densities of at least 400 Wh/kg.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: China is already ahead in commercializing next-generation chemistries, which cuts into any technology-leapfrog thesis for Western startups.
insights.locator: For sodium-ion development, the pipeline

insights.claim: China's 2015-2019 MIIT 'white list' admitted only Chinese battery makers to NEV subsidy eligibility, shielding CATL and BYD from Korean and Japanese competitors until they reached scale. Tesla's Shanghai Gigafactory was then approved as a 'catfish' to push domestic producers to raise their game.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: A template for protect-then-expose industrial policy that other countries are now trying to copy.
insights.locator: Consumer incentives in this period

insights.claim: China's NEV penetration rose from about 5% of passenger vehicle sales in 2020 to over 50% in 2025, and the NEA reports energy storage capacity grew more than fortyfold during the 14th Five-Year Plan. NEVs still drove almost 80% of China's battery demand in 2025.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: Battery storage is the next demand leg, but it must now compete in power markets without mandated deployment.
insights.locator: Second, the economic growth benefits

themes.theme: South Korea's chaebol export model under strain

insights.claim: LG Energy Solution, SK On and Samsung SDI ran at about 50% utilization in 2025 under intensifying Chinese competition, despite LGES plans to grow EV battery output from 173.5 GWh in 2021 to over 1,000 GWh by 2030.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: Low utilization signals margin pressure and slower capex at Korean cell makers.
insights.locator: Domestic Market and Innovation (South Korea)

insights.claim: South Korean firms held about 30% of the global EV battery market by the end of the 2010s through state-chaebol coordination. The sector remains heavily dependent on imported graphite, lithium and nickel intermediates, and high-nickel chemistries make up over 80% of domestic cathode output.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: Korea is exposed to Chinese chokepoints on upstream inputs and is weak in LFP, the chemistry now winning EV and storage share.
insights.locator: By the end of the 2010s

insights.claim: The 2022 U.S. Inflation Reduction Act pushed Korean battery makers to localize in the U.S., backed by KEXIM and K-Sure guarantees for plants such as LG Chem's cathode plant in Tennessee and the SK On-Hyundai joint venture in Georgia. Korea also hedged by building in Europe, including SK On's Hungary plant.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: Korean battery makers are heavily exposed to swings in U.S. EV policy.
insights.locator: The U.S. Inflation Reduction Act of 2022

insights.claim: Falling EV demand, especially in the U.S., is pushing Korean manufacturers toward energy storage systems. The Lee Jae Myung administration links ESS to a 'full-stack' AI and energy strategy and is funding about KRW 280 billion ($204 million) in next-generation battery R&D, including sodium-ion for stationary storage.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: Watch Korean cell makers retooling lines from EV to ESS and LFP; demand from AI data centers is the bull case.
insights.locator: One market trend to watch

insights.claim: From July 2026 South Korea scores EV subsidies on a points basis heavily weighted toward domestic supply-chain content, which works as a de facto localization incentive.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: Korea is joining the trend of content-based protection in EV subsidies.
insights.locator: Effective July 2026, Korea introduced

insights.claim: Japanese firms' global EV battery market share fell from 51.7% in 2015 to 21.1% in 2020 and to around 1% in 2022, as automakers bet on hybrids, efficient combustion engines and fuel cells while Chinese overcapacity grew.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: A cautionary case of an incumbent technology leader losing a market through strategic misallocation.
insights.locator: Policy Background (Japan)

insights.claim: METI's 2022 Battery Industry Strategy targets 150 GWh a year of domestic capacity, 600 GWh of global capacity held by Japanese firms, a 20% global share and a pack price of JPY 10,000/kWh by 2030. METI says domestic capacity was about 120 GWh in early 2024.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: The government is supporting supply, but demand has not followed.
insights.locator: The Battery Industry Strategy sets three goals

insights.claim: Slowing U.S. EV sales led Toyota to postpone its Fukuoka battery plant beyond its 2028 target and Nissan to cancel its Kyushu plant outright. Japan's EV share of new car sales fell from 3.29% in 2023 to 2.12% in 2024, against 24.6% in China.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: The weak domestic EV market caps the scale of Japanese battery makers and keeps them reliant on export demand.
insights.locator: However, the ripple effects of slowing EV sales

insights.claim: Nine members of Japan's Battery Association for Supply Chain, including Hitachi, formed Swiftfab Energy Systems in April 2026. Its subsidized factory, due by the end of 2030, aims to cut equipment costs by 70% to compete with Chinese factories.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: A consolidation test of whether Japan can close the gap with China on manufacturing cost.
insights.locator: Hitachi, jointly established a battery production hub

insights.claim: Japan's EV purchase subsidy lifted January-August 2026 EV sales to 81,158 units, 2.3 times the prior year, but it exhausted its budget so fast that METI is ending applications early in December 2026.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: Japanese EV demand depends on subsidies, so expect a demand air pocket after December 2026.
insights.locator: The purchase subsidy has yielded a positive result

insights.claim: Many of the next-generation chemistries Japan bet on in 2020, such as fluoride-ion, zinc anode and multivalent-ion batteries, are not where innovation is happening today. Japan is concentrating on lithium-metal and solid-state as long-term bets, and Toyota and Kyoto University aim to put a fluoride-ion solid-state battery in EVs by 2035.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of Japan's technology-picking record; its solid-state timelines run long.
insights.quote: However, many of these technologies on which the government placed bets in 2020 are not the areas of innovation today.
insights.locator: In 2020, then prime minister Yoshihide Suga

themes.theme: EU: from ecosystem creation to execution failure risk

insights.claim: By end-2025 Europe had about 140 GWh of actual cell supply against about 305 GWh of installed capacity and about 327 GWh of demand. Non-EU-owned producers supplied about 130 GWh and EU-owned gigafactories only about 10 GWh.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: Europe's battery industry runs on Korean and Chinese producers, and nameplate capacity overstates its real output.
insights.locator: By the end of 2025, Europe had nearly 140 GWh

insights.claim: Northvolt's bankruptcy and the sale of its assets to U.S. lithium-sulfur firm Lyten exposed Germany to potential losses of up to EUR 620 million in public funds. The Heide plant had received EUR 902 million in aid plus a EUR 600 million KfW convertible bond, which raises questions about grants that are not tied to production.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: Europe is likely to shift toward performance-based aid, such as the EUR 1.5 billion Battery Booster loans, rather than capex grants.
insights.locator: Germany has focused on underwriting the capital-expenditure risk

insights.claim: Hungary drew over 60 battery projects worth EUR 26.5 billion in FDI, including CATL's 100 GWh Debrecen plant backed by EUR 800 million in state aid, yet Hungarian battery production fell 51% in 2024 as Chinese and Korean producers competed for the same OEM contracts. CATL indicated it would not share know-how and planned to rotate about 2,000 Chinese workers through its EU plants.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: Courting FDI without requiring technology transfer delivers volume but little local capability, which is why the EU is moving toward conditions on FDI.
insights.locator: Hungary had Europe’s most concentrated FDI-led hub

insights.claim: China reportedly paused investments in EU states that backed the 2024 countervailing duties on Chinese EVs and rewarded those that did not. Spain abstained, and CATL then chose Zaragoza for its joint venture with Stellantis.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: Chinese battery FDI is being used as a geopolitical lever to divide EU member states on trade policy.
insights.locator: Chinese battery investment in the EU

insights.claim: EU demand signals are weakening: the March 2025 Automotive Action Plan let carmakers average 2025 compliance over 2025-2027, and the December 2025 Automotive Package proposes replacing the 2035 100% zero-emission target with a 90% tailpipe reduction. Battery storage was only about 7% of European battery demand in 2025, down from 9%.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: Softer mandates put demand for European battery plants at risk of shortfall.
insights.locator: However, the European Commission’s March 2025 Automotive Action Plan

insights.claim: The key near-term EU signpost is the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act, whose Made in EU requirements and conditions on FDI technology transfer and ownership, aimed mainly at Chinese investment, could create a lead market for EU batteries. Defense and storage may diversify demand.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: A test of whether Beijing will allow advanced battery technology to be transferred to Europe.
insights.locator: The most important near-term signpost

insights.claim: Europe's production is about 92% nickel-cobalt-manganese and about 3% LFP (2025), and the region has a midstream cathode shortage. The two most commercially advanced European next-generation battery firms anchored their commercial facilities in South Korea and India, not Europe.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: Europe is mismatched on chemistry with the LFP trend and is losing next-generation scale-up to other regions.
insights.locator: Europe’s strong market preference

themes.theme: U.S. overbuild, lock-in and pivot to storage and defense

insights.claim: The U.S. has 404 GWh of operational or near-operational cell capacity plus 655 GWh under construction, so over 1 TWh could be running by 2030. Repealing the IRA EV subsidy roughly halved projected domestic demand.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: The U.S. faces cell overcapacity and stranded-asset risk at EV-focused plants; watch utilization and plant pauses.
insights.locator: Domestic Market and Innovation (United States)

insights.claim: Of roughly 30 U.S. cell facilities, 13 are partly or fully run by South Korean conglomerates and 10 involve European or Japanese partners. Cell investment hit nearly $40 billion in 2024, against under $4 billion for all domestic minerals production.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: The U.S. battery buildout depends on foreign-partner joint ventures; the gap is upstream minerals, especially graphite.
insights.locator: Of the thirty or so facilities

insights.claim: Because the U.S. market is nearly self-sufficient in incumbent cell capacity, next-generation battery firms face lock-in risk and may be confined to niches such as drones, eVTOL and defense. Carnegie counts at least 30 U.S. next-generation startups, mostly in San Francisco and Boston.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: This caps the addressable market for venture-backed U.S. battery startups; defense procurement is their swing demand.
insights.locator: Further, the U.S. market being nearly sufficient

insights.claim: The second Trump administration supports only stationary storage, defense and upstream minerals, not EVs, as with the DoE's $500 million for battery supply chains. It has not used targeted battery tariffs, and the planned Biden-era 25% tariff on graphite was never implemented.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: Storage and defense batteries are the parts of the U.S. market that still get policy support.
insights.locator: During the second Trump administration, policy support

insights.claim: The Pentagon's goal of procuring 1 million drones by 2027 or 2028, together with flexible-power demand from the AI boom, could give unexpected tailwinds to high-energy-density chemistries and stationary storage in the U.S.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: Defense and AI data-center power are emerging demand drivers for battery makers that are pivoting away from EVs.
insights.locator: During the second Trump administration, other drivers

insights.claim: U.S. battery signposts include whether the anti-EV agenda escalates, for example through an EV tax in the highway bill, and whether a U.S.-China grand bargain reshapes tariffs on batteries and minerals and inbound Chinese FDI.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: Binary policy risk for U.S. battery plants; a U.S.-China deal could open the door to Chinese LFP licensing.
insights.locator: Key policies and signposts to consider

themes.theme: Canada's multi-alignment and India's import dependence

insights.claim: Canada built its battery strategy on integration with the U.S. supply chain, pairing Canadian minerals with the U.S. market through LG and Volkswagen deals worth CAD 28.2 billion in production-linked payouts. Weaker U.S. EV demand has paused Honda's 36 GWh plant and $1.6 billion of Korean cathode investments.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: Canadian midstream projects are hostage to U.S. EV demand and to the USMCA renegotiation.
insights.locator: Domestic Market and Innovation (Canada)

insights.claim: Under Mark Carney, Canada dropped its ZEV mandate in February 2026 for a looser 75%-by-2035 EV target and agreed to admit 49,000 Chinese-made EVs at MFN tariff rates in exchange for lower tariffs on canola. That move toward battery 'multi-alignment' risks clashing with U.S. Foreign Entity of Concern rules, which require 60% non-FEOC content rising to 85% by 2030.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: Chinese involvement in Canadian battery supply chains could make Canadian products ineligible for U.S. credits, a friction point in USMCA talks.
insights.locator: The government does not view China solely in adversarial terms

insights.claim: India's $2.08 billion PLI-ACC scheme targeted 50 GWh of cell capacity by 2025, but only 1.4 GWh was installed by October 2025 and participants were being penalized for delays. India still imported almost all its cells, 85% of them from China.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: India's localization is far behind plan, so Chinese cells and technology licenses will keep dominating Indian supply.
insights.locator: In 2021, the Production-Linked Incentive

insights.claim: India could have 30 gigafactories by 2030 if commitments materialize, following $7.5 billion of manufacturing investment in 2020-2025, but analysts project domestic production will meet only about 13% of cell demand by 2030. Tamil Nadu (138.9 GWh) and Gujarat (76.2 GWh) are the leading planned hubs.
insights.speaker: Milo McBride
insights.so_what: India's battery growth is a slow, licensed-technology story that relies on Chinese and Korean equipment.
